chapter_title: Understanding Activities and the Android App Structure
chapter_summary:
Every screen in an Android application is typically represented by an `Activity`. Think of an `Activity` as a single, focused thing that the user can do. For example, if you have a messaging app, one activity might display a list of conversations, another might show the messages within a specific conversation, and yet another might allow the user to compose a new message. While it's technically possible to cram a lot of functionality into a single activity, it quickly becomes unwieldy, difficult to maintain, and provides a poor user experience. Android's design encourages breaking down your app's functionality into distinct activities, each managing its own user interface and responding to user interactions.

When an activity starts, it's pushed onto a *back stack* maintained by the Android system. This stack operates on a "last-in, first-out" principle. When the user navigates from Activity A to Activity B, Activity B is pushed onto the stack. If the user then presses the device's Back button, Activity B is popped off the stack, and Activity A resumes. This mechanism ensures a predictable navigation flow and allows users to easily retrace their steps through your application. Understanding this back stack is crucial for designing intuitive navigation.

The lifecycle of an `Activity` is a series of states it can be in, from creation to destruction, managed by the Android system. Key lifecycle callbacks include `onCreate()`, `onStart()`, `onResume()`, `onPause()`, `onStop()`, and `onDestroy()`. The `onCreate()` method is particularly important; it's where you perform basic application startup logic that should happen only once for the entire life of the activity, such as setting the user interface with `setContentView()` and initializing variables. `onStart()` means the activity is becoming visible to the user, `onResume()` means it's in the foreground and interacting with the user, `onPause()` means it's partially obscured, `onStop()` means it's no longer visible, and `onDestroy()` means it's about to be terminated. Properly managing resources within these lifecycle methods, such as releasing network connections or saving user data, is critical for app stability and performance, preventing memory leaks and ensuring a smooth user experience.

All activities in your application must be declared in the `AndroidManifest.xml` file. This manifest is like your app's passport, providing essential information to the Android system about your app's components, permissions, and hardware requirements. For an activity, the declaration typically looks like this:

```xml
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    package="com.example.myapp">

    <application
        android:allowBackup="true"
        android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher"
        android:label="@string/app_name"
        android:roundIcon="@mipmap/ic_launcher_round"
        android:supportsRtl="true"
        android:theme="@style/Theme.MyApp">

        <activity android:name=".MainActivity"
            android:exported="true">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>

        <activity android:name=".DetailActivity" />
        <!-- Other activities go here -->

    </application>
</manifest>
```

In this example, `MainActivity` is declared with an `intent-filter` that includes `android.intent.action.MAIN` and `android.intent.category.LAUNCHER`. This special combination tells the Android system that `MainActivity` is the primary entry point for the application, the one that should appear in the device's app launcher. Any other activity, like `DetailActivity`, does not need these filters unless it also serves as an independent entry point. Forgetting to declare an activity in the manifest is a very common beginner mistake that will lead to a `ActivityNotFoundException` crash when you try to start it. Always double-check your `AndroidManifest.xml` when adding new activities.

Understanding the structure and lifecycle of activities is foundational for building robust Android applications. It allows you to manage the state of your app effectively, respond to system events, and ensure that your app behaves predictably as users navigate through its various screens.

screens.title: Understanding Activities and the Android App Structure
screens.subtitle: How screens, lifecycle callbacks, and the manifest shape app navigation and behavior

narration.text: In this chapter we learn what an Activity is, how Android manages screen-to-screen navigation, and where each activity is declared so the system can run it. An Activity represents a single, focused thing the user can do — often a single screen. You will see how Android keeps track of the screens you visit with a back stack, and how lifecycle callbacks like onCreate and onPause let you prepare and release resources safely. We will also examine the AndroidManifest. xml file to see how activities are declared and how one activity becomes the app's entry point through an intent-filter. You will study concrete examples: a messaging app split into list, conversation, and compose activities; an AndroidManifest snippet that marks MainActivity as the launcher; and a simple hands-on task to add a second activity and verify the manifest. Along the way we'll call out a common beginner mistake — forgetting to declare an activity — and the crash it causes. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to explain the role of activities, map lifecycle callbacks to practical tasks like saving state, and confirm that your activities are known to the system. Think about a small app you might build and which screens would become separate activities.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Activities are the primary units of user interaction and must be declared in the manifest; lifecycle callbacks and the back stack determine how they start, pause, and end.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Understanding Activities
Understanding Activities and the App Structure
Why activities, lifecycle, and the manifest matter for predictable navigation and stable apps.
In this lesson

Explore Key Topics

Lifecycle

Quick start

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will gain four measurable abilities related to Android activities. First, you will be able to explain what an Activity represents in an application and describe the lifecycle callbacks that guide its behavior. This matters because the lifecycle determines when to initialize views and when to release resources to avoid leaks. Second, you will understand how multiple activities compose an app, so you can design screens that are focused and maintainable rather than cramming unrelated features into one large screen. Third, you will identify the parts of AndroidManifest. xml that relate to activities, including how the system learns about the classes that can be launched. And fourth, you will distinguish the app's entry point from subsequent activities, recognizing the intent-filter combination that makes an activity the launcher. Each objective is practical: you'll see examples, validate declarations that Android Studio generates, and check for common mistakes. As you study, ask yourself how your app's screens map to activities and where lifecycle callbacks should save and restore state.

keyIdea.text: Explain activities and lifecycle, design apps as multiple activities, declare activities in the manifest, and identify the app entry point.

screens.title: What is an Activity?
screens.subtitle: A single, focused thing the user can do — typically a screen

narration.text: An Activity models a single, focused task that the user performs in your app. Think of each Activity as a screen with a lifecycle of its own: it controls the user interface, handles user interaction, and coordinates with other app components. For example, in a messaging app you might have a ConversationsActivity that shows the list of conversations, a ChatActivity that shows messages for one conversation, and a ComposeActivity that lets the user write a new message. This separation keeps each screen's code focused and maintainable. A common misconception is treating activities as only UI containers; they are also responsible for lifecycle-aware decisions, like when to register listeners or start background work. When you design your app, prefer small, single-purpose activities rather than one monolithic activity. Small activities make it easier to reason about state, simplify testing, and map exactly to the user's tasks. However, don't over-split — too many tiny activities can complicate navigation. The practical takeaway is to assign an activity when a user performs a distinct task that benefits from its own lifecycle and navigation entry. Ask yourself: does this screen represent a discrete user goal? If yes, an activity is appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An Activity is the unit that represents one focused user task or screen and defines how that screen behaves over time.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is an Activity?
Definition & Analogy
An Activity represents one focused thing the user does. Imagine each Activity as a separate page in a book: each page has its own content, and you can flip between pages to continue reading.
Example: Messaging app
ConversationsActivity, ChatActivity, ComposeActivity — each maps to a single user goal and UI layout.
Common misconception
Activities are not only view holders; they manage lifecycle decisions like registering listeners and releasing resources.
Key Takeaway

Choose activities for distinct user tasks to keep UI and code focused and maintainable.

Concrete scenario
If a user taps a conversation in a list, that action moves them from the conversations screen to a dedicated chat screen. This transition is typically implemented by starting a new Activity that displays messages for the selected conversation.
Check your understanding
  • Would this screen represent a distinct user goal?
  • Does it need its own lifecycle management for resources?
  • If yes to both, prefer a dedicated Activity.

screens.title: The Back Stack and Navigation
screens.subtitle: How Android records screen navigation with a LIFO stack

narration.text: Android uses a back stack to maintain the order of activities a user visits. The back stack behaves like a last-in, first-out stack: when you start Activity B from Activity A, Activity B is pushed onto the stack. If the user presses Back, Activity B is popped and Activity A resumes. This makes forward and backward navigation predictable and aligns with user expectations on mobile platforms. A concrete example: tap a conversation in the list to open ChatActivity; ChatActivity sits on top of the stack. Press Back to return to the conversation list and resume its state. A common misconception is assuming Back always destroys the previous activity; in many cases the previous activity remains in memory and only lifecycle callbacks like onResume are invoked. Understanding the back stack is important when you design multi-screen flows and when you manage state between screens. When starting new activities, you can also pass data via intents, but remember that navigation flow still follows the stack unless you alter it through flags. Consider whether a screen should be added to the back stack or replace the current entry; this decision affects how users retrace steps through your app. How will users naturally return to where they started?

keyIdea.title: Back Stack
keyIdea.text: Activities are pushed and popped on a LIFO back stack, which determines how users navigate backward through screens.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Back Stack
LIFO navigation model
The back stack records each started activity so pressing Back reverses the most recent navigation. This preserves the user's history within your app's task.
Activity A: Conversations
User selects a conversation.
Activity B: Chat
ChatActivity is pushed onto the stack. Back pops ChatActivity and resumes ConversationsActivity.
Misconception check
The previous activity is not always destroyed; usually it is stopped and later resumed, so retain important UI state between onPause and onResume.
Practical implications
  • Decide if a screen should be a new Activity based on whether users will navigate back to the previous context.
  • Use intent extras to pass data between activities while preserving the back stack order.
  • Use special flags only when you need to modify the default back stack behavior.
Key Takeaway

The back stack gives users a predictable path back through your app; design screen flows with this behavior in mind.

screens.title: Activity Lifecycle — Overview
screens.subtitle: States and callbacks from creation to destruction

narration.text: The Activity lifecycle describes the states an activity transitions through and the callback methods the system calls at each transition. The key callbacks you will use are onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, and onDestroy. onCreate is where you perform one-time setup such as setContentView and initializing variables. onStart means the activity is becoming visible. onResume means it is now in the foreground and interacting with the user. onPause indicates the activity is partially obscured and should commit unsaved changes or pause animations. onStop means the activity is no longer visible, a place to release heavier resources. onDestroy signals the activity is about to be destroyed and you should clean up remaining resources. A common student mistake is assuming onDestroy is always called; the system may kill the process without calling it under low-memory conditions, so save critical state earlier, for example in onPause or onSaveInstanceState. Understanding this sequence helps you choose where to start or stop services, register or unregister listeners, and save user data safely so that your app behaves reliably across navigation and interruptions. Activity Lifecycle — Overview means use lifecycle callbacks to initialize ui, pause interactions, release resources, and save state in a predictable sequence of states.. In practical terms, states and callbacks from creation to destruction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle map
keyIdea.text: Use lifecycle callbacks to initialize UI, pause interactions, release resources, and save state in a predictable sequence of states.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Lifecycle Overview
Lifecycle timeline
onCreate()
One-time setup like setContentView and initial variable binding.
onStart()
Activity becomes visible but not yet in the foreground.
onResume()
Activity now interacts with the user; resume animations and listeners here.
onPause() / onStop()
Pause ongoing actions, save quick state, then release heavy resources in onStop.
onDestroy()
Clean up final resources, though this may not always be called before the process is killed.
Practical guidance
  • Initialize UI and single-run setup in onCreate.
  • Start animations or foreground listeners in onResume, pause them in onPause.
  • Release network connections or heavy resources in onStop.
  • Save critical state in onPause or onSaveInstanceState because onDestroy may not be called.
Key Takeaway

Map each piece of setup and cleanup to the appropriate lifecycle method to keep your app responsive and leak-free.

screens.title: onCreate() — Where to set up your UI
screens.subtitle: Perform one-time initialization safely

narration.text: onCreate is the central place to perform the one-time startup tasks for an activity. Typical actions here include calling the method that sets the view layout and initializing important variables. For instance, you call setContentView to bind the XML layout to the activity and findViewById or view binding to locate UI elements. You might also initialize view models or restore saved instance state if available. A concrete example: when you create a ChatActivity, onCreate is where you inflate the chat layout, attach the message list adapter, and set up click handlers for the send button. A common misconception is to start heavy background work directly in onCreate; prefer lightweight setup here and start heavier tasks in onStart or onResume if they require the activity to be visible. Also avoid assuming onCreate will be called only once across process restarts; state restoration may require reading saved state. The practical rule: use onCreate for layout and initial wiring, then use later callbacks to start work that depends on the activity being visible. How will you structure onCreate in your next screen so it remains concise and safe?

keyIdea.title: onCreate rule
keyIdea.text: Do one-time setup and UI binding in onCreate, but defer heavy visible work to onStart or onResume.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › onCreate()
Code pattern
<-- Kotlin-like pseudocode example for onCreate -->
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
  super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
  setContentView(R.layout.activity_chat)
  // bind views, initialize adapters
  // restore UI state if savedInstanceState is not null
}
This pattern shows the essential steps: call the superclass, set the layout, then bind views and initialize lightweight structures.
Practical example
In ChatActivity, inflate the chat layout, attach your messages adapter to a RecyclerView, and set click listeners for sending messages. Defer heavy data loads until the activity is visible.
Common mistake
Starting blocking or long-running work directly in onCreate can delay UI display. Prefer lightweight wiring here and start heavier tasks in onStart or onResume.
Key Takeaway

Keep onCreate focused on view binding and simple initialization; timing-sensitive work belongs later in the lifecycle.

screens.title: Visible and Foreground State: onStart() and onResume()
screens.subtitle: When to register listeners, start animations, and begin interacting

narration.text: After onCreate, an activity moves into visible and foreground states handled by onStart and onResume. onStart signals the activity is becoming visible; use this callback to acquire resources needed while the UI is visible but not yet interactive. onResume signals the activity is in the foreground and ready for user interaction — resume animations, register UI listeners, and start components that require an active UI. For example, if your ChatActivity shows live incoming messages through a socket or subscription, onResume is the right time to attach or resume the listener so the user sees updates. A common misconception is to register long-running listeners in onCreate and forget to unregister them; this can cause leaks when the activity is stopped. The pattern to follow is symmetric: register or start in onResume/onStart and unregister or pause in onPause/onStop. This symmetry ensures you do not hold onto resources while the activity is not visible and prevents unnecessary battery or memory use. Consider whether the work must run only while the activity is in the foreground or can safely continue while it is merely visible, and choose the appropriate callback accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Visibility callbacks
keyIdea.text: Use onStart and onResume to begin visible and interactive work; unregister or pause in onPause and onStop to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › onStart & onResume
When to start visible work
  • onStart: prepare resources needed while visible but not yet interactive.
  • onResume: resume or attach listeners for interactive updates and animations.
  • onPause/onStop: detach listeners and stop animations to conserve resources.
Example: start a live message subscription in onResume so the chat receives updates only while users are actively viewing the conversation.
Practical checklist
Attach UI listeners in onResume
Start animations in onResume and pause in onPause
Unregister receivers in onPause or onStop
Key Takeaway

Match resource start/stop to visibility and foreground state to avoid wasted work and memory leaks.

screens.title: onPause(), onStop(), onDestroy() — Saving and Releasing
screens.subtitle: How to save state and release resources before an activity is stopped

narration.text: onPause, onStop, and onDestroy are the callbacks you use to save transient state and release resources when an activity goes out of view or is terminated. onPause is your earliest reliable signal that the user is leaving the activity; use it to commit quick, essential data—like unsent message drafts or UI state—because onDestroy might never be called if the system terminates the process. onStop indicates the activity is no longer visible; this is the place to release heavier resources such as large bitmaps, network connections, or sensors. Finally, onDestroy is for last-chance cleanup when the activity is explicitly finished, but again, it is not guaranteed under all system conditions. A concrete example: in a chat app, save the text the user typed in onPause so it can be restored if they return, close a socket connection in onStop to free network resources, and unregister any observers in onDestroy. A common error is assuming onDestroy will always run. The practical rule is to persist important state earlier and always balance resource acquisition with a corresponding release in these lifecycle callbacks. onPause(), onStop(), onDestroy() — Saving and Releasing means persist critical state in onpause and release heavy resources in onstop; do not rely on ondestroy to always run.. In practical terms, how to save state and release resources before an activity is stopped. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Resource management
keyIdea.text: Persist critical state in onPause and release heavy resources in onStop; do not rely on onDestroy to always run.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Pause, Stop, Destroy
When to save and release
  • onPause: save quick and essential UI state so it survives process death.
  • onStop: release heavy resources like network connections, large caches, or sensors.
  • onDestroy: final cleanup for resources that were not released earlier, but not guaranteed to run.
Example: save an unsent message draft in onPause, close the message synchronization socket in onStop, and unregister observers in onDestroy if still present.
Common mistakes
Relying on onDestroy for important persistence is risky. Also, failing to release heavy resources in onStop can cause memory pressure and poor performance for the user and the device.
Key Takeaway

Persist critical state early and always pair resource acquisition with timely release to keep apps stable.

screens.title: AndroidManifest.xml and Activity Declarations
screens.subtitle: How the manifest tells Android about each activity

narration.text: AndroidManifest. xml is the app's configuration file where you declare the activities the system can launch. Each activity must appear as an tag inside the element. For example, typical entries name MainActivity and a detail or secondary activity. The manifest also contains intent-filters that tell the system which activity is the app's main entry point: an intent-filter pairing android. intent. action. MAIN with android. intent. category. LAUNCHER causes the activity to appear in the device's app launcher. A concrete manifest snippet shows these parts and is what the system reads at install time to build the app's capabilities. A frequent beginner mistake is forgetting to add the activity tag, producing an ActivityNotFoundException when starting the activity. Another detail shown in example manifests is the android:exported attribute: launcher activities commonly set exported="true" while non-launcher activities often remain exported="false" by default. Always open the manifest to verify new activities appear after you create them. This way you ensure Android can find and instantiate your screens at runtime. AndroidManifest.xml and Activity Declarations means list every activity in androidmanifest.xml; use intent-filters to mark the launcher entry and avoid activitynotfoundexception.. In practical terms, how the manifest tells android about each activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Manifest role
keyIdea.text: List every activity in AndroidManifest.xml; use intent-filters to mark the launcher entry and avoid ActivityNotFoundException.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Manifest Walkthrough
Example manifest
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    package="com.example.myapp">

    <application
        android:allowBackup="true"
        android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher"
        android:label="@string/app_name"
        android:roundIcon="@mipmap/ic_launcher_round"
        android:supportsRtl="true"
        android:theme="@style/Theme.MyApp">

        <activity android:name=".MainActivity"
            android:exported="true">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>

        <activity android:name=".DetailActivity" />

    </application>
</manifest>
This snippet shows MainActivity declared with an intent-filter that makes it the launcher entry, and a DetailActivity declared without the launcher filter so it is launched only when your code starts it.
Checklist and notes
  • Verify every activity you add appears under <application> in the manifest.
  • Only give MAIN and LAUNCHER to the true entry activity so the system shows it in the launcher.
  • Missing an activity tag commonly causes ActivityNotFoundException — always inspect the manifest after creating activities.
Key Takeaway

The manifest is the app's passport; ensure it lists and configures each activity so Android can launch and manage it properly.

screens.title: Entry Point vs Other Activities
screens.subtitle: What makes MainActivity the launcher and how others differ

narration.text: The app's entry point is the activity the system launches when the user taps the app icon. This is determined by an intent-filter that pairs android. intent. action. MAIN with android. intent. category. LAUNCHER inside the activity declaration in AndroidManifest. xml. That combination tells the operating system to show this activity in the device's application launcher. Secondary activities, like a DetailActivity or SecondActivity, do not include that intent-filter and are launched by explicit intents from within your app or by other components. A concrete example: MainActivity has the MAIN and LAUNCHER intent-filter and exported="true" so it appears in the launcher, while SecondActivity is declared without intent-filter and often remains exported="false" by default, meaning it is not independently listed in the launcher. A common misconception is to add MAIN/LAUNCHER to multiple activities expecting different entry behavior. Doing so makes multiple launchable icons and complicates navigation. Another mistake is assuming exported attributes are optional in all cases; launcher activities typically must be exported so the system can start them. The practical rule: mark a single activity as the launcher entry and keep other activities declared but without launcher filters unless you explicitly intend multiple entry points.

keyIdea.title: Launcher vs internal activities
keyIdea.text: Pair MAIN with LAUNCHER in the manifest to make an activity the app entry; other activities are started by code and typically don't need launcher filters.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Entry Point vs Others
Launcher activity
An activity with an intent-filter including android.intent.action.MAIN and android.intent.category.LAUNCHER becomes the app's entry visible in the device launcher. It usually sets android:exported="true" so the system can start it.
Example
MainActivity declared with MAIN and LAUNCHER appears as the app icon the user taps.
Secondary activities
Activities without the MAIN/LAUNCHER filter are launched from code or other components. They do not appear in the launcher and often keep exported="false" by default for safety.
Misconception check
Don't add MAIN/LAUNCHER to multiple activities unless you intentionally want more than one launcher entry point.
Key Takeaway

Reserve MAIN+LAUNCHER for the single app entry point; design other activities to be started from within the app.

screens.title: Common Manifest Mistakes and Runtime Errors
screens.subtitle: Why ActivityNotFoundException happens and how to avoid it

narration.text: A frequent runtime error for beginners is ActivityNotFoundException. This happens when your code tries to start an activity that the Android system cannot find, usually because the activity was not declared in AndroidManifest. xml. For example, you might create a DetailActivity class but forget to add an tag under. When you then call startActivity with an intent for DetailActivity, the system throws ActivityNotFoundException because it never recorded the class during installation. To avoid this, always open app/src/main/AndroidManifest. xml after adding an activity and check for the corresponding activity declaration. Android Studio often updates the manifest automatically when you use the Empty Activity template, but manual confirmation is a good habit. Another mistake is misnaming the android:name attribute or using the wrong package prefix; ensure the manifest name matches your activity class. The practical routine: after creating an activity, confirm the manifest, run the app, and if a crash occurs, inspect the log for ActivityNotFoundException and verify the manifest entry. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Manifest Mistakes
Why ActivityNotFoundException occurs
This exception happens when the system cannot find an activity to handle an explicit intent, most commonly because the activity was not declared in the manifest or the android:name is incorrect.
Checklist to fix the error
  1. Open AndroidManifest.xml and confirm the activity tag exists under <application>.
  2. Verify the android:name attribute matches the activity class name and package.
  3. If using Android Studio templates, confirm the studio added the entry as expected.
Example
If DetailActivity is missing from the manifest, starting it will crash. Add <activity android:name=".DetailActivity" /> to resolve the issue.
Key Takeaway

After creating an activity, always confirm its manifest declaration to prevent runtime crashes.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the core points to remember. First, an Activity models a single user-focused task or screen; design activities for distinct user goals to keep code clean. Second, the Activity lifecycle—onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy—dictates where to initialize UI, start and stop visible work, and release resources. Third, Android uses a back stack that pushes activities when you navigate forward and pops them when you navigate back, ensuring predictable backward navigation. Each concept influences how you structure code and manage state. Keep these concepts in mind as simple design rules: use activities for separate screens, map setup and teardown to lifecycle callbacks, and verify each activity appears in the manifest. screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for building multi-screen apps

narration.text: Here are three compact reminders to carry forward. First, activities are the screens of your app; give each distinct user task its own activity to keep responsibilities clear. Second, lifecycle callbacks are your map for when to create, resume, pause, and destroy resources; prefer saving essential state in onPause and releasing heavy resources in onStop. Third, the AndroidManifest. xml must list every activity; forgetting to declare a new activity is the usual cause of an ActivityNotFoundException. Keep these three checks in your development routine: screen design, lifecycle mapping, and manifest verification. They make multi-screen app development much more reliable and maintainable.
